extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers learning to interpret and critique poetry (teachers of practical criticism)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for close reading and practical criticism of poems, focusing on distinguishing four functions of meaning (Sense, Feeling, Tone, Intention), handling figurative language, and avoiding common reading errors. Emphasises diagnostics, multiple readings, and sensitivity to genre/context.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Four Kinds of Meaning (Sense, Feeling, Tone, Intention)
rubrics_metrics.description: Language has four distinct but interacting functions: Sense (what is said), Feeling (the conative‑affective aspect — emotions, will, desire, pleasure‑unpleasure), Tone (the speaker's attitude to the listener), and Intention (the speaker's aim or purpose).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat each function as separable for analysis; failures may occur in any one and may entail aberrations in the others. Each function influences the language used in ways additional to the others and deserves separate consideration (see Part IV and Appendix A references). Examples and protocols illustrate typical failures and interactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sense (Function i: clarity and coherence of statement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sense is the presentation of facts, objects of thought, and the precise meaning of words and syntax — the element by which a poem conveys propositional content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sense is often the poet's chief instrument for controlling feeling and must be accurately grasped; misreading the sense loses most of a poem's value. However, sense cannot always be wrenched free and paraphrased prosaically — beware turning a poem into a prose doctrine. In some genres (scientific treatise) sense should predominate; in others (poetry) it may be subordinated or manipulated for effect. Examine syntax and literal meanings first; disentangle sense before rejoining other factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feeling (conative‑affective function)
rubrics_metrics.description: Feeling covers emotions, attitudes, will and desire expressed by the language — the emotional colouring or 'personal flavour' a writer gives to subject‑matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the feelings the poem expresses and whether language successfully manipulates or evokes those feelings. Many poetic statements exist primarily to produce feeling rather than to assert literal truth; readers who treat them as propositions misunderstand their function. Note when feeling subordinates sense deliberately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone (attitude to the listener/audience)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tone reflects how the speaker arranges words depending on the audience — the attitude or relation the writer adopts toward listeners/readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how tonal choices (register, jokes, cajolery, formalities) are shaped by the intended audience. Tone can change wording, rhythm and rhetorical strategy; correct appreciation requires awareness of the audience relation and of tactics such as tact in popular exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intention (authorial purpose and effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: Intention is the writer's aim or the effect he or she seeks to promote (conscious or unconscious) and includes aims that operate through and beyond Sense, Feeling and Tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine what the author is trying to do (state facts, evoke feeling, reorient opinion, win acceptance, etc.) because judgement of success depends on this. Intention may govern emphasis, arrangement, and 'plot' and is especially important in dramatic and semi‑dramatic literature. Note that some reader mistakes stem from failing to consider intention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify predominant function(s) for the piece and genre
rubrics_metrics.description: Different genres and contexts give different precedence to the four functions (e.g., scientific treatise gives priority to Sense; popular exposition may subordinate Sense to intelligibility, Feeling and Tone; political speeches give predominance to Intention and Feeling/Tone).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting, ask which function is dominant in the instance at hand and judge choices against that standard. Recognise appropriate sacrifices (e.g., simplification in popularisation) and inappropriate ones (irrelevant aims such as defending a thesis). Adjust expectations and evaluative criteria to genre/context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple readings are necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Most poetry requires several readings to allow its varied factors (sense, feeling, tone, metre, figures) to fit together and be grasped.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expect all poetry to come fully to the reader at first reading; if metre or verse‑form distracts, silence that 'band' while disentangling sense, then reintroduce other elements. Readers who claim initial comprehension of all good poetry are overconfident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the twin dangers: careless 'intuitive' reading and prosaic 'over‑literal' reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Two common reading errors are (a) careless, intuition‑based readings that ignore syntax and sense, and (b) prosaic, over‑literal readings that force poetic language into strictly propositional prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both approaches wreck understanding (the 'Symplegades' or 'justling rocks'). Test readings against syntax and poetic use; neither guesswork nor crude paraphrase should be allowed to dominate interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not treat figurative statements as literal propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Many poetic statements are not contributions to doctrine but means to manipulate and express feelings; treating metaphors or images as literal claims is a category error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a poem asserts metaphoric images ('My soul is a ship') assess them as expressive devices rather than as factual propositions. Distinguish readers who take statements 'seriously' (find them silly) from those who swallow them as aesthetic philosophy. Context and function determine proper interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetical liberty to distort sense must be justified by effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets may distort, mix, or even produce logical nonsense in their statements if the effect (expressive, emotive, imaginative) justifies the breach of literal coherence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the emotive/intended effect is achieved; nonsense is admissible only when its contribution to feeling or tone compensates for loss of literal coherence. Consider whether the poet's other aims make the liberty legitimate; if not, count it a defect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate mixed metaphors and figurative mixtures for internal coherence and efficacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Mixtures in metaphors (combining different ingredients/figures) can succeed if the mind can handle the combination and the ingredients preserve their efficacy; they fail when parts cancel one another or produce internally inconsistent imagery (a 'fire and water' mixture).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse whether the components of a mixed figure blend to reinforce the intended feeling or whether they neutralise or contradict each other. Check for independent efficacy of each image and for contexts that allow fusion without loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check internal logical coherence of figurative images
rubrics_metrics.description: Inspect figurative claims for glaring internal inconsistencies or impossibilities (e.g., 'strings made of the lightning of Spring nights' as impossible/contradictory), recognising that some impossibilities may be defensible if they produce the intended effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List and test the separate flaws of a figure rather than dismissing it wholesale; determine whether each inconsistency derives from a central liberty or is a series of unrelated cracks. Use logical analysis to see whether any justification or compensating effect exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider intertextual influence and reader familiarity with other poets
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers' responses are affected by acquaintance with other poets; a passage may echo or reflect another poet (obsession/echo) and readers familiar with the source may respond differently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether liking/disliking stems from original effect or from recognition/echo (e.g., Swinburne influence). When possible compare reader reactions before and after exposure to likely influences to isolate genuine merit from learned enthusiasm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate sensitivity and discrimination with words
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding the best poetry requires nicety, imaginativeness and deftness in taking the sense of words — a subtle capacity for word meanings and their poetic uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop fine discrimination in word‑sense to avoid both literalist disdain and naïve swallowing. This quality is essential for sensitive appreciation and prevents damaging indulgence in neglecting verbal precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware and diagnose 'literalism' as a specific obstacle
rubrics_metrics.description: A common misconception is to demand scientific precision or literalism of poetic language, treating metaphors as factual claims and condemning imagery as exaggeration or childish 'fancy'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast literalism with its opposite error to find middle cases where accuracy and figurative liberty are combined. Use examples to show how literal demands would invalidate much good poetry and to teach readers how poetical sense differs from scientific sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trace cross‑connections: failures in one function may mislead in others
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the four functions interpenetrate, a mistake in apprehending one (e.g., Sense) often causes distortions in assessments of Feeling, Tone or Intention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approach diagnosis like repairing a complex device or a psychological clinic: examine interdependencies and be alert to how a primary failure propagates. Do not treat misreadings as isolated; test alternative hypotheses about source of error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate personification and temporal/logical liberties contextually
rubrics_metrics.description: Personification and other devices grant wide imaginative liberties (e.g., making night and dawn contemporaneous); they are permissible provided they contribute meaningfully to the poem's intention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use imagination and common sense judiciously to justify such liberties; ask whether these devices add pictorial or emotive value or merely distract. Do not rely solely on 'common sense' to condemn poetic transpositions; judge by effect and contribution to intention.
